description: A curated handbook distilling Masahiro Sakurai's game design philosophy, development insights, and practical techniques from his YouTube channel. Covers game essence, design principles, UI/UX, visuals, animation, audio, player experience, team management, work ethic, marketing, programming, and specific design tips. Designed for game developers, designers, and enthusiasts seeking actionable wisdom.
audience: Game developers, designers, producers, artists, programmers, and enthusiasts of all skill levels.
routing_rules: If query is about core game mechanics, risk-reward, difficulty, or player motivation, route to 'Game Essence' or 'Game Design Principles'.
If query is about UI, controls, menus, or accessibility, route to 'UI/UX Design'.
If query is about graphics, effects, or visual polish, route to 'Visual & Graphics'.
If query is about animation, character motion, or hit feedback, route to 'Animation & Motion'.
If query is about sound effects, music, or audio design, route to 'Audio Design'.
If query is about player experience, tutorials, or time management, route to 'Player Experience'.
If query is about development workflow, project management, or technical tools, route to 'Development Insights'.
If query is about team leadership, communication, or team culture, route to 'Team Management & Workflow'.
If query is about personal productivity, creative process, or professional attitude, route to 'Work Ethic & Mindset'.
If query is about marketing, trailers, or community engagement, route to 'Marketing & Communication'.
If query is about programming practices, parameter tuning, or debugging, route to 'Programming & Tech'.
If query is about specific design techniques like hit stop, screen shake, or explosion effects, route to 'Design Specifics'.

entries.title: Risk and Reward: The Core of Game Essence
entries.summary: Game essence is defined by the trade-off between risk and reward. Classic examples like Space Invaders and Super Mario show how proximity to danger increases both tension and payoff.

entries.title: Squeeze and Release
entries.summary: Game fun originates from applying pressure (enemies, puzzles) and then releasing it with rewards. Design a clear pressure-release cycle.

entries.title: Game Essence in RPGs
entries.summary: RPGs balance risk and reward through dangerous areas, resource management, and weakness systems.

entries.title: Game Essence in Falling-Block Puzzle Games
entries.summary: The key difference between pure puzzles and falling-block games is risk vs return. Time pressure and speed create tension.

entries.title: Game Essence in Shooting Games
entries.summary: Risk-reward in shooters: positioning near enemies yields higher rewards; understand why a mechanic is fun, not just imitate.

entries.title: Do We Really Need Enemies?
entries.summary: The core of game satisfaction is the pressure-release cycle. Enemies are a common pressure source, but you can use other mechanisms like puzzles, time limits, or resource management.

entries.title: Falling Sells the Feeling of Flight
entries.summary: To make flying feel exhilarating, introduce the risk of falling (or other penalties). Players appreciate freedom more when there is danger.

entries.title: Difficulty and Player Retention
entries.summary: Games are most exciting on the edge of victory and defeat, but excessive difficulty can drive players away. Provide non-humiliating escape routes like difficulty adjustment or skip options.

entries.title: Player Guidance and Freedom
entries.summary: Decide how much to guide the player. Explicit instructions help weaker players but reduce freedom. More open designs encourage exploration but may lead to confusion.

entries.title: Mandatory Strategies and Strategic Balance
entries.summary: Nintendo often designs boss fights with clear mandatory strategies. This provides focus but can feel tutorial-like. Balance forced guidance with player autonomy.

entries.title: Game Essence in Strategy Games
entries.summary: Strategy games use rock-paper-scissors style counters, cost differences, and positional elements to create meaningful decisions.

entries.title: Average and Mediocre Are the Same Thing
entries.summary: Over-balancing leads to homogenization. In Smash, characters have distinct strengths and weaknesses with win rates ranging only from 47% to 51% across 87 characters—proving individuality and balance can coexist.

entries.title: More Game Essence Means Less Broad Appeal
entries.summary: High risk-reward design increases game essence but decreases broad appeal. Examples from Mario and Kirby illustrate this trade-off.

entries.title: Difficulty Balance and Player Agency
entries.summary: Games are most fun at the edge of win/lose, but being unable to complete is frustrating. Provide difficulty options, skip, or scaling to avoid abandonment.

entries.title: Teach by Doing
entries.summary: Design tutorials that let players learn through natural gameplay rather than separate practice levels.

entries.title: Teaching Players How to Play
entries.summary: Avoid long text tutorials and boring practice fields. Embed learning into gameplay via initial levels with contextual prompts.

entries.title: Making Tutorials Feel Natural
entries.summary: Tutorials should be integrated into gameplay, not separate training. Use visual cues but ensure they cover all key configurations.

entries.title: Reward System Design
entries.summary: Make rewards visible and desirable. Show progress bars (XP to next level) to motivate players. Use clear, immediate feedback for every action.

entries.title: Design Rewards with Consumption
entries.summary: Pair rewards with meaningful consumption mechanics to maintain player motivation.

entries.title: Consider Rewards First
entries.summary: Rewards are the primary driver of player motivation. Design the reward system early, including numerical, collectible, and unlockable rewards.

entries.title: Keeping Rewards in Sight
entries.summary: Display progress toward rewards to motivate players; use scarce high-impact items that encourage saving.

entries.title: Good Errands and Bad Errands
entries.summary: Fetch quests can be satisfying if designed well: appropriate rewards, small incentives along the way, multiple strategies, quick return, compelling story.

entries.title: Fetch Quest Design
entries.summary: Good fetch quests satisfy five conditions: appropriate reward, short gratification spans, freedom of approach, quick extraction, and anticipation of future benefit.

entries.title: Readability vs Style
entries.summary: Balance user-friendly clarity with stylish visuals, but never sacrifice readability for the sake of aesthetics.

entries.title: HUD Design
entries.summary: Design HUD elements that inform without distracting; consider dynamic visibility and thematic integration.

entries.title: Accessibility Options
entries.summary: Provide comprehensive accessibility settings to make the game playable by a wider audience.

entries.title: Loading Screen Design
entries.summary: Handle loading screens by blending them into gameplay or keeping them informative and brief.

entries.title: Text Rendering & Localization
entries.summary: Consider language-specific text sizes and allow localizers to adjust text animation parameters for better emotional impact across cultures.

entries.title: Menu Color Coding
entries.summary: Use distinct color schemes for different menu sections to aid navigation, but limit colors per screen to avoid chaos.

entries.title: Icon Sizing by Importance
entries.summary: Make icons larger for frequently used functions and smaller for secondary ones, but watch out for text overflow in different languages.

entries.title: Make Important Elements Bigger
entries.summary: Scale UI icons by importance to intuitively guide users. Larger icons for frequent actions, smaller for rare ones.

entries.title: Color-Coding Your Game UI
entries.summary: Use color coding to differentiate UI sections but avoid clutter; colors must suit the game's tone.

entries.title: Adding Help Text to Menus
entries.summary: Menu items need explanatory text, but avoid using the same words as the item itself. Use simple, jargon-free language.

entries.title: Making Things Clear, Even Without Words
entries.summary: Use icons, character graphics, and default actions so players can understand and play even without knowing the language.

entries.title: Maps Are Game Screens, Too
entries.summary: Warns that players often stare at maps instead of the main screen. Use transparent maps, enhance main screen with directional cues, and use environmental landmarks.

entries.title: Menus Define Your World
entries.summary: UI and font choices dramatically change a game's target audience and world feel. Ensure readability and holistic design.

entries.title: Let Them Skip, Let Them Pause
entries.summary: All non-interactive sequences must be skippable and pausable. Modern players expect control over their time.

entries.title: Button Settings and Key Configuration
entries.summary: Provide button remapping even in simple games. Use a graphical controller UI; allow duplicate bindings; save configurations per player.

entries.title: Button Responsiveness
entries.summary: Every button press must yield a reaction—even if trivial—to avoid player confusion. Map confirm to multiple buttons for accessibility.

entries.title: Fast Menu Selection
entries.summary: Proposes adding a scroll wheel to game controllers for rapid menu navigation. The principle of fast, satisfying input persists.

entries.title: Character Silhouette and Readability
entries.summary: Distinct silhouettes are crucial for character recognition in fast-paced games. Adjust characters to ensure their profile is immediately identifiable.

entries.title: Graphical Polish and Consistency
entries.summary: Small adjustments to characters and environments elevate the final product. Pay attention to foot placement, color palettes, and animation direction.

entries.title: Effective Use of Post-Processing
entries.summary: Modern hardware allows frame buffer and shader effects that dramatically improve visual quality. Use subtly to unify art style.

entries.title: Dealing With Color Disparity
entries.summary: Monitor inconsistencies cause color differences; calibrate tools, use neutral lighting, and rely on a reference display for final approval.

entries.title: Making Things Look Miniature
entries.summary: To create a miniature effect, blur top/bottom (shallow depth of field), increase saturation, and reduce blue (remove air perspective).

entries.title: Get the Sense of Scale Right
entries.summary: Large objects in games often look like miniatures. Fix this by avoiding repetitive textures, reducing saturated colors, controlling specular highlights, and using normal maps consistent with size.

entries.title: Low-Resolution Pixel Art Techniques
entries.summary: For small sprites, use odd pixel widths to get a center line for smoother curves. Use highlight/edge manipulation for material feel.

entries.title: The Basics of Pixel Art
entries.summary: Fundamental pixel art techniques: use odd pixel dimensions for circles, checkerboard dithering for gradients, and add one extra color for highlights.

entries.title: Final Output Post-Processing
entries.summary: On high-end hardware, post-processing is more important than raw polygon count. Frame buffer manipulation defines visual quality.

entries.title: Color Accessibility
entries.summary: Ensure game elements are distinguishable for colorblind players by using brightness differences and color blindness simulation filters.

entries.title: Team Art Style Unification
entries.summary: When mixing characters from different franchises, unify via: lowered saturation, consistent texture detail, adjusted body proportions, redesigned details, and uniform expression style.

entries.title: A Fight Between Live Action and Animation
entries.summary: Five techniques to unify cartoon and realistic characters: desaturation, balanced texture, proportion adjustment, re-design, realistic motions.

entries.title: Graphics and Fun
entries.summary: Good graphics enhance immersion and player engagement, especially in atmospheric games and online storefronts.

entries.title: F: Graphics 1 (Category Compilation)
entries.summary: Compilation of graphics supervision tips: draw reflected light, emphasize hit-detection areas, allocate performance budget, adjust scale via texture/lighting, use Photoshop for quick mockups.

entries.title: Manga-like Visuals
entries.summary: Embrace non-realistic techniques: mouths visible sideways, eyes seen through glasses frames, squash-and-stretch from animation. Use shape animation for elastic effects.

entries.title: Let Your Characters Shine
entries.summary: Prevent effects from obscuring characters: in 2D, use higher render priority; in 3D, adjust depth test or render order. Use edge lights.

entries.title: Distinguishing Between Major and Minor Elements
entries.summary: Allocate graphical resources wisely: prioritize screen center, character detail over background, use LOD, cut unnecessary detail.

entries.title: Emphasize Objects with Collision
entries.summary: Make collision-enabled areas visually prominent; use atmospheric perspective and reduced contrast for non-collision areas.

entries.title: Draw the Light, Not the Asset
entries.summary: Graphic drawing should represent reflected light using color variations, spray gradients, and atmospheric perspective.

entries.title: Make It Pop: Visual Effects
entries.summary: Use color addition for glow but avoid overuse; combine with hard-edged effects and dark elements for contrast.

entries.title: Flash, Blast, and Smoke: Explosion Effects
entries.summary: A classic explosion effect consists of three phases: a quick flash, a central blast, and smoke to fade out. Consider background color and screen shake.

entries.title: Hit Stop Mechanics
entries.summary: Hit stop is a brief pause on attack impact that dramatically improves combat feel. Ultimate implements seven special variations for nuanced feedback.

entries.title: Eight Hit Stop Techniques
entries.summary: Details seven special hit stop techniques used in Super Smash Bros. Ultimate: larger shake on receiver, no hitbox offset, directional shake control, amplitude decay, adjustable pause length, smooth pose transition, slight attacker movement.

entries.title: Stop for Big Moments
entries.summary: Hit stop and boss stop enhance impact. Early games already used these techniques. Apply to various genres.

entries.title: Breaking Down Attack Animations
entries.summary: Frame attack animation into four phases: idle, start-up, attack, follow-through. Emphasize strong first frame, hit stop on contact, and cancel frames in follow-through.

entries.title: Always Keep Attack Collision in Mind
entries.summary: Attack collision areas are often larger than visual models to ensure hits connect. Animators must design motions with collision in mind.

entries.title: Attack Poses
entries.summary: In action games, the pose during hitstop is critical for feel. Make poses exaggerated: cross the body's midline, avoid symmetry, twist torso, clear silhouettes.

entries.title: Center of Gravity Shift
entries.summary: Offset the rotation pivot of an object from its geometric center to make movement feel organic and lively.

entries.title: Sprite Cycling for Wobble
entries.summary: Cycle a sprite's display position through a predefined pattern to simulate unsteady flight or wobble.

entries.title: Damage Animation Transition
entries.summary: When a character takes damage, the first frame of damage animation should be hit instantly (often via hit stop), then transition smoothly via interpolation from hit pose.

entries.title: Extreme Keyframes for Sharp Animation
entries.summary: To keep 2D-style sharpness in 3D, exaggerate key poses beyond what looks natural; reduce intermediate frames to avoid softness.

entries.title: Facial Expressions Exaggeration
entries.summary: Facial expressions need to be stronger than you think; show upper and lower whites of eyes, avoid closed teeth, exaggerate mouth shapes.

entries.title: IK and FK Usage
entries.summary: Use IK for foot placement and end-effector tasks; FK for expressive arcs. Exaggerate joint rotations beyond 180° for impact.

entries.title: Rotation on Two Axes
entries.summary: Single-axis rotation looks robotic. Always combine at least two axes and stagger their timing. Add anticipation and adjust speed curves.

entries.title: G: Animation 1 (Category Compilation)
entries.summary: Comprehensive animation workflow: start with text-based move list, use action figures for reference photos, break moves into four stages, exaggerate poses, use cancel frames.

entries.title: Establishing Characters Through Their Design
entries.summary: Character design should prioritize silhouette recognizability, exaggeration of key features, and consistent poses to convey personality.

entries.title: Flipped Animation
entries.summary: Mirror character poses and actions so opponents face each other toward the screen, improving visual information and spectacle in fighting games.

entries.title: Animation Blending
entries.summary: Blend animations to create smooth transitions. Keep blend times short (0.1-0.3s) to preserve crispness. In 3D, use layered blending.

entries.title: Motion Blur
entries.summary: Motion blur enhances speed feel but can reduce clarity. Use sparingly; provide intensity slider in options. Prefer artistic blur or hardware bloom.

entries.title: Squashing and Scaling in Animation
entries.summary: Apply squash and stretch to add weight and energy. Maintain volume conservation. For extra quality, combine with blend shapes or mesh deformation.

entries.title: Too Much is Just Right
entries.summary: For action animations, exaggerated motion that risks breaking the model is actually better; most attack animations are too limited.

entries.title: Assigning Animations
entries.summary: Use move lists and action figure photography to specify actions; each character about 70-80 photos.

entries.title: Animation Interpolation Pitfalls
entries.summary: Warn against over-relying on automatic interpolation when converting 2D to 3D. Manual keyframe adjustment and reducing intermediate frames produces sharper actions.

entries.title: Audio Importance
entries.summary: No masterpiece has bad audio. Sound effects and music are as critical as graphics and gameplay; they are what players remember most.

entries.title: BPM Selection
entries.summary: Match music BPM to the desired intensity: fast (130-170) for action, slower for exploration.

entries.title: SFX Priority
entries.summary: Set volume levels for sound effects based on gameplay importance: K.O. sounds should be loudest, walking softest.

entries.title: Multi-Device Audio Testing
entries.summary: Test audio on a range of devices from high-end headphones to cheap TV speakers to ensure it sounds good everywhere.

entries.title: Modern Game Music
entries.summary: With complex modern graphics, music should take a backseat; use ambient sounds and subtle variations of a main theme to create atmosphere.

entries.title: Realism vs Exaggeration in SFX
entries.summary: Choose sound style based on game's visual tone: exaggerated for arcade/action, realistic for simulation/horror.

entries.title: Voice Recording
entries.summary: Keep voice lines short and avoid excessive chatter during gameplay. Localize voices per region.

entries.title: Music Production Flow
entries.summary: When commissioning music, let composers choose tracks they are passionate about, but supervise to ensure melody identity is preserved.

entries.title: Sound Effect Design: Attack and Reverb Control
entries.summary: For impactful sound effects, ensure the attack (initial peak) is strong and prominent, and avoid excessive reverb that muddies subsequent hits.

entries.title: Reference Music Cautions
entries.summary: When using existing music as reference, avoid being overly constrained by it; allow composers creative freedom.

entries.title: Audio as Fiction and Non-Fiction
entries.summary: Game sound design needs balance between exaggeration and realism. Fighting games benefit from exaggerated sounds, while realistic games need authenticity.

entries.title: The Original Piece is Always Right
entries.summary: When remixing game music, respect the original as heard by players, even if it defies music theory.

entries.title: Strike a Balance with Sound Effects
entries.summary: Prioritize sound effect volume based on gameplay impact: K.O. sounds loudest, then hit sounds, then special moves, then movement.

entries.title: Make the Tempo Match the Game
entries.summary: Music tempo should align with gameplay intensity; e.g., 130-170 BPM for battles, slower for exploration.

entries.title: Listen in Various Environments
entries.summary: Always test audio on multiple devices: headphones, cheap TV speakers, PC speakers. Avoid changing reference headphones once set.

entries.title: Famicom and NES Audio
entries.summary: Overview of Famicom/NES sound hardware: two pulse waves, one triangle, one noise, one DPCM. Later disk system added waveform memory; expansion chips caused regional differences.

entries.title: Using Other Songs for Audio Reference
entries.summary: Using existing songs as audio references can help but may limit creativity. Allow composers creative freedom.

entries.title: Be Mindful of the Time Players Are Giving You
entries.summary: Player time is a cost, not free. Avoid advertising long playtimes upfront; make the game so engaging that players willingly invest time.

entries.title: Say No to Slow!
entries.summary: Players universally dislike slowness: slow movement, long wait times, idle periods. Minimize all avoidable delays.

entries.title: Make Retries Quick
entries.summary: Minimize downtime after failure. Fast retries keep players engaged and increase tolerance for difficulty.

entries.title: Death Relief
entries.summary: In competitive games, players may feel relief when defeated due to quick respawns. Design for both sides to have fun.

entries.title: Praise the Player
entries.summary: Celebrate player actions with visual, audio, or text praises—even for minor achievements—to boost motivation.

entries.title: Praise Players Constantly
entries.summary: Use positive feedback to celebrate player actions, even for opponent's mistakes.

entries.title: A World Without Footprints: Spoiler-Free Experience
entries.summary: To maximize personal discovery and emotion, avoid all trailers, guides, and gameplay videos until after finishing the game.

entries.title: Enjoying Games Without Spoilers
entries.summary: Sakurai prefers to walk on untouched snow: avoid any spoilers, walkthroughs, or let's plays.

entries.title: Respecting Player Time
entries.summary: Games that boast hundreds of hours of content can backfire; time is a cost. Developers should respect player time by allowing skips, fast travel, efficient saving.

entries.title: Embracing Games of All Eras
entries.summary: Sakurai shares his childhood experiences and encourages players to explore older games to appreciate the medium's evolution.

entries.title: The Fun in Picking Sides
entries.summary: Choosing a side increases engagement in competitive games. Use prediction mechanics for emotional investment.

entries.title: Branching Tastes
entries.summary: Player interests become more diverse with age. Younger players form a broad 'trunk' market; older ones split into niches.

entries.title: That Was Then, This Is Now
entries.summary: Each era has merits; modern games are more polished but older ones often innovated more. Encourage trying new games.

entries.title: Game Opening
entries.summary: Your game must hook players within the first 3 minutes. Skip lengthy intros; jump into core gameplay immediately.

entries.title: Just Let Them Play
entries.summary: Game should show core fun within first 3 minutes; avoid lengthy prologues; let players play immediately.

entries.title: High Difficulty and Roguelike Appeal
entries.summary: High difficulty games thrive because players want to see what comes next. Simply copying difficulty without strong motivation leads to frustration.

entries.title: Fuel Motivation with Anticipation
entries.summary: High difficulty is acceptable if players have a strong desire to see what comes next.

entries.title: Being Kind to Beginners
entries.summary: When facing a clearly new player, tone down your skill level to give them a fun experience. Design your game to ease beginners in naturally.

entries.title: Handling Development Setbacks
entries.summary: Game cancellations and delays happen. Sakurai emphasizes learning from failure, knowing when to cut losses, and maintaining team morale.

entries.title: Role of the Director
entries.summary: Sakurai describes his role in Smash Bros: providing vision, solving key design hurdles, and personally playtesting. A director must be hands-on and make final decisions.

entries.title: Team Building and Communication
entries.summary: Sakurai shares how he assembled the Smash Bros X team from external companies. Good communication and respect are key.

entries.title: Making Your Game Easy to Tune
entries.summary: Parameter externalization: store all tunable numbers in Excel, use formulas for relationships, hide seldom-changed values, automate conversion.

entries.title: Bug Testing Systems
entries.summary: Establish structured bug tracking: unified ROMs, severity ranking (S/A/B/C), assignment to specialists, regression testing. Use automated testing for large games.

entries.title: Debug Mode
entries.summary: Implement a debug mode early with features like invincibility, camera control, stat adjustment. Use a single controller for all debug functions.

entries.title: Storage and Cable Management
entries.summary: Organize game collections and development hardware with custom cabinets, cable management, and label printers.

entries.title: Transparency Features
entries.summary: Development tools that allow making parts of a character model transparent to better see animations. Useful for debugging and clean screenshots.

entries.title: Naming Conventions
entries.summary: Use consistent, English-friendly naming to avoid confusion between development terms and player-facing names.

entries.title: Parameter Externalization
entries.summary: Store tunable numbers in external files like Excel, not hard-coded, to allow quick iteration without recompiling.

entries.title: Ticket System
entries.summary: Use a ticket system to manage all tasks so that every job has an owner and status, preventing tasks from falling through the cracks.

entries.title: Frame Rates
entries.summary: Frame rate is the basic unit of game time, usually 60fps standard. 30fps common but 60fps smoother. NTSC/PAL differences affect speed; variable frame rate can maintain consistency.

entries.title: Units of Speed
entries.summary: Speed in games is defined by distance/time units. In 2D pixel games, dots/frame; in 3D, real-world units like km/h but scaled with character size.

entries.title: Learn to Count Frames!
entries.summary: Understanding frame length is crucial for timing game actions. With 60fps, counting '1 and 2 and 3' approximates 30 frames.

entries.title: Put Parameters in Brackets
entries.summary: Distinguish between program logic and adjustable parameters. Use brackets in specs to denote parameter names and circles to mark values needing tuning. Store in separate files.

entries.title: Name Files Logically
entries.summary: Use consistent naming conventions: 'Attack' for normal moves, 'Special' for specials, direction codes (N, S, L), strength numbers. Use English.

entries.title: Staying Organized with Hierarchical Outlines
entries.summary: Use outline view to structure ideas hierarchically, ideal for personal planning.

entries.title: Creative Solutions Under Hardware Constraints
entries.summary: Tight memory and processing limits force elegant design. Example: Kirby's 512KB used symmetric graphics and pre-programmed enemy paths.

entries.title: Kirby Development Secrets
entries.summary: How original Kirby was made with extreme ROM constraints: mirrored sprites, no terrain collision for enemies, prototype designs already matching final.

entries.title: Mushi King Development
entries.summary: A small-team LSI game featuring beetle raising and battling. Balance growth phases, hidden specs add depth, watch for platform speed differences.

entries.title: Up is Down, Down is Up
entries.summary: As a director or lead, you are not above the team; you are requesting their help. Treat everyone with respect and speak politely.

entries.title: Director as Trimmer
entries.summary: A director's job includes cutting unnecessary or overly risky tasks to keep the project on track.

entries.title: Early Trouble Reporting
entries.summary: Encourage team members to report problems as early as possible, so director can adjust the plan.

entries.title: Lessons from Mr. Iwata
entries.summary: Satoru Iwata's leadership: hands-on problem-solving, open communication, service-oriented spirit.

entries.title: Supervision Workflow
entries.summary: Handle supervision requests via email processed in order of arrival, replying same day. Set aside 'no supervision' periods for focused work.

entries.title: Decision-Making Principles
entries.summary: In meetings, make decisions immediately. Avoid postponing conclusions even if imperfect; course-correct later if needed.

entries.title: Debug Ticket System
entries.summary: Manage bugs with ticket system: severity ranking (S/A/B/C), assign to developers, verify fix, archive. Use unified ROM version for testing.

entries.title: Role of Director vs Producer
entries.summary: Director owns game content and has final say on creative. Producer handles budget, schedule, team management, external relations.

entries.title: Finish Everything Within the Day
entries.summary: Manage review requests via email, process in arrival order, reply same day. Dedicate no-review time for personal work.

entries.title: How Multiple People Work on One File
entries.summary: Files stored on server with lock/edit/unlock. Large files cause bottlenecks. Merge conflicts may require manual resolution; ancestor regression can occur.

entries.title: Sharing Info Within a Team
entries.summary: Three methods: daily dev log (with comments), daily screenshot, periodic project showcase presentations.

entries.title: Explain Ideas to Everyone at Once
entries.summary: All team members relevant to a feature gather for a single explanation session, reducing misinterpretation.

entries.title: Don't Rely on a 'Plan B'
entries.summary: In design documents, propose the single best solution you've arrived at, then refine through team feedback.

entries.title: Canceled Games
entries.summary: Project cancellation happens. Developers should be aware of business pressures and contribute beyond assigned tasks to help project succeed.

entries.title: Spec Changes
entries.summary: Avoid spec changes when possible, but be flexible; when you find a problem, report immediately and decide quickly with full information.

entries.title: Decide on the Spot
entries.summary: Don't postpone decisions. In meetings, urge decision-makers to decide immediately unless key person absent.

entries.title: Stay True to Your Concept
entries.summary: The original concept is a beacon. Long development can blur focus, but never abandon core vision. Changing direction mid-dev wastes resources.

entries.title: Specification Changes
entries.summary: Avoid unnecessary spec changes. When needed, weigh pros and cons quickly. Communicate impacts to team.

entries.title: Ten People Can Produce Seven People's Work
entries.summary: A 10-person team typically produces only 7 people's work due to management overhead. Experienced members transitioning to leadership reduce personal output but improve team efficiency.

entries.title: Mastering Up
entries.summary: Master Up is the final delivery milestone. It's not always celebratory; often involves tough compromises. Acknowledge effort and accept imperfections.

entries.title: The Story of Sora Ltd.
entries.summary: Sora Ltd. is Sakurai's personal company for contracting. No employees, no hiring, does not accept resumes. Business model: no advance payment, only revenue share.

entries.title: Company-Supported Game Development
entries.summary: Working within a company provides stable salary, shared risk, and support. Recognize the value of organizational infrastructure.

entries.title: Majority Should Not Rule
entries.summary: In creative decisions, majority voting tends to produce safe, mediocre results. A well-informed director should make final calls.

entries.title: Directors and Producers
entries.summary: Director oversees content decisions; producer manages team, budget, schedule, marketing. Both must collaborate.

entries.title: Don't Wait to Speak Your Mind
entries.summary: Express dissatisfaction or improvement ideas immediately within the team, not after completion. Pair criticism with solution. Establish 'Opinion Officer' role.

entries.title: Jobs in Game Development
entries.summary: Overview of typical roles: Director, Planner, Programmer, Model Artist, Artwork, Motion, Effect, Sound, UI, Technical Supporter, Manager, Monitor, Debugger.

entries.title: Sora's Work-From-Home Strategies
entries.summary: When Smash Ultimate switched to remote work, issues included poor desks, slow internet. Solution: give each employee budget to choose own equipment. Expect 30% productivity drop.

entries.title: Make Games Because You're Good At It
entries.summary: Make games because you're good at it, not just because you love them. Work is work; be reliable, respect constraints, focus on delivering a great player experience.

entries.title: Just Do It Already!
entries.summary: The hardest part is starting. Overcome procrastination by immediate action. Motivation follows action.

entries.title: Broad Input, Broad Output for Creatives
entries.summary: To improve work quality, intentionally broaden input (play games, watch films, read) and output (write, share, speak). Make it a daily habit.

entries.title: Keep Your Internal Pressure High
entries.summary: Keep early ideas secret to build creative pressure, leading to more passionate and refined outputs.

entries.title: The Power of Suggestion
entries.summary: Imagine a terrifying object chasing you to trigger flight response; set tight deadlines to boost efficiency. Running away from deadlines works better than chasing goals.

entries.title: Competition and Abundance in Game Development
entries.summary: The game industry is fiercely competitive, yet abundant with opportunities. Developers should persist, and players should appreciate the effort.

entries.title: Never Get Into Fights
entries.summary: The game industry is small; burned bridges will come back. Avoid arguments, gossip, and leaving on bad terms.

entries.title: Elementary School Play Testers
entries.summary: Invite children to playtest early builds for unfiltered feedback on engagement, difficulty, and fun.

entries.title: Column Persistence
entries.summary: How Sakurai maintained a weekly column for 18+ years: output easily, limit time per session, keep it light without over-commitment.

entries.title: Try Telling That to the Player
entries.summary: Develop with player as priority; don't sacrifice player experience for development convenience.

entries.title: Game Development Isn't a Game
entries.summary: Game development is professional work; even if you don't like it, complete it with player happiness as goal.

entries.title: Presentations Are All About Speed
entries.summary: Demos and pitches must be fast and dense. Cut all fluff. Show the game early, summarize quickly.

entries.title: You'll Forget the Hardship, But the Game Will Endure!
entries.summary: Game development is hard, but the pain fades while the game remains. Remember that millions may play your game.

entries.title: Directors Need to Be Unique
entries.summary: Great game directors share a trait: they notice nuances others miss and think differently. Cultivate your own perspective.

entries.title: Creators Change, Too
entries.summary: Developers may leave the game industry but find success elsewhere. Don't assume they've failed; change is natural.

entries.title: The Power of Words
entries.summary: Spoken words shape reality through influence on mindset and actions. Avoid negative talk; channel negativity into improvement.

entries.title: Treat Marketing as Essential
entries.summary: A great game must also be well-known; invest equally in development and promotion.

entries.title: Ensure Product Image Matches Reality
entries.summary: Never mislead consumers; trailers and screenshots must accurately represent the final game.

entries.title: Use Demos Judiciously
entries.summary: Demos can be effective but require significant effort and may spoil experience if not well-crafted.

entries.title: Create Shareable Character Reveal Videos
entries.summary: Design reveal trailers that are exciting, self-contained, and shareable without context from the main game.

entries.title: Produce Trailers Step-by-Step
entries.summary: Trailer creation involves multiple iterations: storyboard, animation, CG, sound, and frequent reviews.

entries.title: Show Gameplay First in Trailers
entries.summary: Begin trailers with actual game footage rather than logos or cinematic intros.

entries.title: Official Websites
entries.summary: Websites remain vital for deep, centralized information; earlier used to correct bias (e.g., Smash Bros.).

entries.title: Smash Bros. DOJO!!
entries.summary: The Smash Bros. DOJO website started as a manual to explain the game's unique appeal, later evolved into official daily-updated news site. Key: consistent, developer-driven updates.

entries.title: Beyond Market Analysis
entries.summary: Market analysis relies on past data and cannot predict future hits. Sakurai advises a skeptical stance: use for reference, not as compass for innovation.

entries.title: Sustaining Information Flow
entries.summary: The 'Smash Bros Ticket' website kept fans engaged with daily updates. Continuous, fresh information builds loyal audience.

entries.title: Marketing is Multiplicative
entries.summary: Development and marketing are like two wheels; both must work for success. Marketing multiplies the value of development.

entries.title: Making and Releasing Game Demos
entries.summary: Demos are effective marketing but costly: require separate builds, version management, risk spoiler leaks. Evaluate resources.

entries.title: Making a Living Making Games
entries.summary: The most direct path into the game industry is to make your own games, starting with clones and iterating based on feedback.

entries.title: Crafting Games Similar to Existing Ones
entries.summary: It's common to make games inspired by existing titles, but you must offer unique appeal that the original doesn't have.

entries.title: Avoiding Comparison in Pitches
entries.summary: When presenting a new game idea, avoid describing it as 'like [existing game]'. Focus on unique value proposition.

entries.title: Making Sequels
entries.summary: Sequels can leverage existing systems but must deliver noticeable improvement over the original to overcome likely sales drop (often 50%).

entries.title: All Stars Return Project
entries.summary: Super Smash Bros. Ultimate's core concept: bring back every previous character. Clear vision and managing constraints.

entries.title: The Price of Games
entries.summary: Games are cheap relative to other entertainment; support developers by buying games directly or playing them via subscription.

entries.title: Fun Beyond Game Essence
entries.summary: Game fun comes from many sources: operation feel, story, fandom, simulation, creativity, rhythm. Designers should blend these.

entries.title: Prep Your Proposals Hot and Fast
entries.summary: Game proposals should be written quickly and concisely while enthusiasm is high. Focus on fun, not lengthy explanations.

entries.title: Writing Game Proposals
entries.summary: Proposal style: each slide has one image and one sentence; can be long (200+ pages) but easy to flip through like a comic. Include categories and progress indicators.

entries.title: Effective Presentation
entries.summary: Demos and pitches must be fast and dense. Cut all fluff. Show the game early, summarize quickly, let gameplay speak.

entries.title: Proposal Writing
entries.summary: Write proposals with one idea per page. Use one image and max two lines of text. Many pages fine as long as each clear.

entries.title: Sound Feedback
entries.summary: When giving sound effect feedback, be specific: 'more attack', 'higher pitch'. Reference known sounds. Vague onomatopoeia like 'gaki' doesn't help.

entries.title: Show Actual Gameplay
entries.summary: Marketing material must show actual gameplay footage early. Avoid long logos, trailers, or intros.

entries.title: Knockback in Super Smash Bros.
entries.summary: Detailed parameters (vector, reaction values) allow precise knockback control for unique victory conditions.

entries.title: Unexpected Results
entries.summary: Optimization can alter game balance. Online updates help, but offline testing is crucial.

entries.title: Online Updates
entries.summary: Modern games are complex; bugs and balance issues are inevitable. Online updates are necessary but should not crutch—first impressions matter.

entries.title: Minimize Display Latency
entries.summary: Ensure your game responds instantly; help players reduce display lag through settings.

entries.title: Manage Remote Work Productivity
entries.summary: Remote development can reduce efficiency; mitigate with proper equipment and processes.

entries.title: Set Up a Lean Company Structure
entries.summary: Small, flexible entities (like a yūgen gaisha) can work well for freelance developers.

entries.title: Plan Budgets Realistically
entries.summary: Be aware of all costs: development, marketing, localization, and hidden expenses.

entries.title: Organize Content with Numbering
entries.summary: Use systematic file naming and folder structures to manage large volumes of assets.

entries.title: CRT Displays
entries.summary: CRT monitors have unique properties: fast response, vibrant colors, interlaced scanning, visible scanlines. Understanding these helps in designing for retro or retro-styled games.

entries.title: Long Ago, Numbers Were Used to Draw Pixel Art
entries.summary: In early microcomputers, pixel art was created by manually entering hexadecimal numbers representing 4x1 pixel patterns.

entries.title: Family BASIC
entries.summary: Explores Famicom's Family BASIC peripheral, a programming environment with 2KB memory, preloaded sprites, battery backup. Author credits it for launching his career.

entries.title: Screen Shake
entries.summary: Screen shake powerfully conveys impact. Tune with camera movement (3D) or post-render move (2D), apply decay and randomness.

entries.title: Visual Effects in Slow Motion
entries.summary: Effects are often too fast to notice but greatly enhance atmosphere. Observing in slow motion reveals detail.

entries.title: Blade Trails
entries.summary: Two main methods: polygon trails (for most swings) and billboard placement (for fast, single-frame swings). Customize trail per character.

entries.title: Billboard Effects
entries.summary: Billboard technique: polygons always facing camera. Used for particles, explosions, and certain objects. Variations like Y-axis billboard and pitfalls.

entries.title: Particle Optimization
entries.summary: Optimize particle effects by shortening lifetime, increasing speed, using composite particles, offsetting emission times, avoiding overlap.

entries.title: Wind Cut Techniques
entries.summary: Weapon trails (wind cuts) via polygonal trail meshes or billboard meshes along the path.

entries.title: H: Effects 1 (Category Compilation)
entries.summary: Covers color additive effects, explosion patterns, screen shake, hitmark design, hitstop behavior, directional hit indicators. Emphasizes combining clear geometric elements with additive layers.

entries.title: The Limitations of Particle Effects
entries.summary: Particle effects can strain performance; optimize by shortening lifespan, staggering spawn times, using pre-baked animation frames instead of real-time particles.

entries.title: Flashing Effects
entries.summary: Flashing effects enhance feel and convey state. Contrast issues with additive blending; solutions like mixing with dark colors or adding shadows.

entries.title: Hit Marks: Designing Impact Effects
entries.summary: Hit marks must be flashy, clear contrast, appear at exact hit point, combine multiple effects, avoid obscuring characters, adjust duration based on game pace.

entries.title: Making Lead-ins Instant and Impactful
entries.summary: 'Kamae' (wind-up) affects responsiveness and impact. Smash Bros. favors immediate pose change on input for quick response, but too little reduces impact. Balance based on online lag.

entries.title: Don't Anchor Your Center Point
entries.summary: Avoid locking camera focal point rigidly to player character. Adjusting Y-axis delay during jumps or shifting forward during action enhances sense of height, speed, and feedback.

entries.title: Modern Quality of Life Features
entries.summary: The Last of Us Part 1 offers extensive accessibility and QoL settings: visual adjustments, controller remapping, subtitle customization, combat assists, and more.

entries.title: A Small Window Into the World
entries.summary: Screen view is only ~30° field of view; affects racing games especially. VR helps for direction-independent games. Design UI considering actual screen usage area.

entries.title: The Fiend's Cauldron
entries.summary: Risk/reward system in Kid Icarus: Uprising where players spend currency to raise difficulty (earn more) or can lower it. Dynamic balancing prevents hard locks.

entries.title: The Potential of One Button
entries.summary: Single-button games can be categorized into four types: rapid fire, timing, speed press, and toggle. Match operation feel to game sense.

entries.title: Let Players Cheat the System
entries.summary: Players naturally seek exploits for advantage. These 'cheats' often become memorable fun. Tolerate small exploits that add emergent gameplay.

entries.title: The Pros and Cons of Leaderboards
entries.summary: Leaderboards give goals and matchmaking, but frustrate non-top players. Use inverted rankings (lower=better) and VIP rooms to soften blow.

entries.title: Customization Lets Your Imagination Play
entries.summary: Five key points: visualize effects, clear pros/cons, easy selection, quick testing, cool design. Customization itself must be fun.

entries.title: It's Easier If They Already Know
entries.summary: Leverage industry-standard controls to reduce learning curve; always allow full button remapping.

entries.title: Clarity vs. Style in UI
entries.summary: UI needs balance between clarity and style depending on game content.

entries.title: Text Size
entries.summary: Ensure text large enough for different languages, especially Japanese; consider adjustable text size options.

entries.title: Handicap Systems
entries.summary: Handicaps balance skill gaps in multiplayer. In Smash Bros., intentional manual handicapping is most effective.

entries.title: Making Work Games Fun
entries.summary: Games lacking traditional risk-reward can still be fun through realistic tasks, clear reward loops, and satisfying progression.

entries.title: Making the Imaginary Feel Real
entries.summary: Virtual worlds become believable through small details: textures suggesting weight, wear-and-tear, and subtle environmental effects.

entries.title: Balancing Ambient Sounds
entries.summary: Ambient sounds have low priority but are essential for immersion. Present during quiet moments, never overpower key effects.

entries.title: Making Effects the Right Size
entries.summary: Effects must be scaled correctly relative to characters. Common mistake: making flames too large, looking like candle flames.

entries.title: Presenting Scores in Meaningful Ways
entries.summary: Raw scores less engaging. Attach to relatable concepts (brain age, total damage) transforms perception. Quick counting feedback enhances satisfaction.

entries.title: Giving Weight to Buttons
entries.summary: Button feel is determined by in-game action parameters (speed, frame rate). Design considering tactile feeling.

entries.title: Down with Lag
entries.summary: Reduce display delay to ensure game experience. Choose low-latency mode and reduce intermediate devices.

entries.title: Game Awards
entries.summary: Game awards should celebrate diversity, not ranking; encourage awards highlighting originality.

entries.title: Super Smash Bros.
entries.summary: Origin of Smash Bros: simplified controls, damage accumulation, using iconic characters to reduce entry barrier.

entries.title: Super Smash Bros. Melee
entries.summary: Development concept: massively power-up original Smash (graphics, audio, content). Used GameCube disk for streaming music, CG cutscenes, figure collection.

entries.title: Super Smash Bros. Brawl
entries.summary: Development insights: online play, single-player mode 'Subspace Emissary', new systems like Final Smash and Assist Trophies, slower pace for casuals, professional test players.

entries.title: Super Smash Bros. for 3DS / Wii U
entries.summary: Dual-platform development with shared systems, unique features per console, technical achievements (60fps + 3D).

entries.title: Kirby's Dream Land: Design Philosophy
entries.summary: First Kirby game deliberately lowered difficulty to guide new players: flight avoids fall deaths, inhaling enemies reduces risk, simple controls.

entries.title: Kirby Super Star: Co-op and Anthology
entries.summary: Two-player master/slave system and anthology structure enhance variety and replay value.

entries.title: Kirby's Adventure: Introducing Copy Abilities
entries.summary: Copy abilities allow beginners to clear easily and experts to explore deeply, enriching character identity.

entries.title: Kirby Air Ride: Development Case Study
entries.summary: A case study on creating with limited time. Core mechanic: drift plus charge-and-release (risk/reward). Focus on variety (City Trial) rather than speedrunning. Vehicles differ only by parameters set by Sakurai.

entries.title: Meteos: Innovation in Puzzle Design
entries.summary: Core innovation flips traditional block-puzzle mechanics: launch blocks upward as propulsion. Each planet has unique shapes, physics, audio.

entries.title: Kid Icarus: Uprising - Innovative Design
entries.summary: A case study in hybrid genre (rail shooter + TPS) on 3DS, with touch-screen aiming, large enemies, full narratives in gameplay.

entries.title: Game & Watch Design Preservation
entries.summary: Showcasing original LCD patterns from Game & Watch used as reference in Smash. Emphasizes preserving historical game assets.

entries.title: Guidelines
entries.summary: Guidelines unify but may restrict creativity. Always question their necessity.
